chapter: Dana Valery and the Glenn Miller band
title: Buddy DeFranco's Glenn Miller Orchestra and the London trip
summary: Joining the DeFranco Glenn Miller band, recording Live in London, strict time and sound, and sharing hotel rooms by ghosting.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Because I had got a call to go — I’m moving this rocking chair — I got a call to go with the Glenn Miller band and they were going to Japan. Now here’s my ticket back. I said, “okay, I’ll go.” And we were going to London as well. So I quit and joined the Buddy DeFranco Glenn Miller Orchestra. And we did a recording, “Live in London” at the Royal Festival Hall. Now this was — I had never been this sick in my life. I was playing two bass drums then and endorsing Ludwig drums. Buddy DeFranco was a pretty serious taskmaster with time. I mean because of the dancers, he didn’t want anybody stumbling over their feet. So there was not a lot of looseness involved with that band and the Glenn Miller office didn’t want to vary too far from the Glenn Miller sound. So it was a learning experience. And I had come out of the Army and I said here I am back in the Army. That kind of thing. I did that — we went to London and I had one steak over there. Everything was fish & chips. The bars were closed at the wrong time. It seemed as though I just couldn’t, you know like they’d close at 2:00 and then we were traveling, and they’d re-

open at 5 and by the time the job ends they were closed. I couldn’t get loaded, I couldn’t do anything. But I’m staying at the London Strand ghosting — we called it ghosting, you ever heard of ghosting?
Um hum. You could explain it though.

Ghosting means that one guy checks into a hotel room and two guys live in it. You break the bed down, one sleeps on the bed spring, and you split the bill. Because the Glenn Miller band didn’t pay for rooms. And I’m on the floor. I wake up on the day of this recording session, of this live concert, which was two concerts which means four sets. We’ve got to do the whole show twice. And “Bugle Call Rag” was one of the tunes and I mean that thing was fast. And I called Buddy DeFranco and I said — my ghost went downstairs and said, “Buddy, I don’t think Danny can even stand up,” which I basically couldn’t. It was food poisoning. I got food poisoning. And I said, “you’ve got to call Ronnie Verrell or somebody. Somebody’s going to have to come in and do this job. I can’t even walk.” And they sent a doctor, which was socialized medicine at the time. And he came up to the room and he said, “this is the strongest thing I have for nausea” and everything else. He gave me a shot. I couldn’t even go over for the sound check. I couldn’t do anything. I just got in a cab and went to Royal Festival Hall and played. Twice. I mean two shows. And I managed to get through it. And it came out on the record although my drum solo on the record that was released on Paramount Records here was cut to a minute and a half. Japan recently released it and it’s an eight minute drum solo. How I did that I’ll never know. Twice, that night. But that was the sickest I’ve ever been on a bandstand in my life, recording live for I don’t know how many people the Royal Festival Hall holds, but on the cover of the record, I’m on the cover of the record with DeFranco.
